title: Redis
subtitle: Single-threaded event loop architecture, core data structures, RDB vs AOF persistence, and Redis Cluster 16,384 hash slots.
keyTakeaways: Redis achieves 100k+ ops/sec using a single-threaded event loop with I/O multiplexing (`epoll`/`kqueue`), eliminating lock contention and context switches (with multi-threaded network I/O in Redis 6+).
Beyond simple strings, Redis provides native atomic data structures: Sorted Sets (`ZSET` skip-list + hash table for leaderboards/rate limiters), Hashes, Streams, and HyperLogLog.
Redis Cluster partitions the keyspace into 16,384 fixed CRC16 hash slots (`CRC16(key) % 16384`) distributed across master nodes without a central proxy.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Redis is a foundational architectural concept in distributed systems. Single-threaded event loop architecture, core data structures, RDB vs AOF persistence, and Redis Cluster 16,384 hash slots. Fundamentally, Because Redis executes commands sequentially on a single thread in RAM, every command (and every embedded Lua script) is atomic by default without needing mutexes. However, this means O(N) commands like `KEYS *`, `SMEMBERS` on a 1M-element set, or slow Lua scripts will block the entire Redis server and cause cascading timeouts.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Redis achieves 100k+ ops/sec using a single-threaded event loop with I/O multiplexing (`epoll`/`kqueue`), eliminating lock contention and context switches (with multi-threaded network I/O in Redis 6+).

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Beyond simple strings, Redis provides native atomic data structures: Sorted Sets (`ZSET` skip-list + hash table for leaderboards/rate limiters), Hashes, Streams, and HyperLogLog.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: In production distributed systems, redis manifests across several distinct architectural classifications, operational modes, and implementation strategies:
bullets: **RDB Point-in-Time Snapshots Only**: Focuses on compact files, minimal disk i/o overhead during normal operation, fastest restart times. Best suited for Pure caches where data can be reconstructed from the primary SQL/NoSQL database..

**Hybrid RDB + AOF (`appendfsync everysec`)**: Focuses on bounds potential data loss to at most 1 second with near-native in-memory performance. Best suited for Session stores, rate limiters, real-time leaderboards, and write-behind buffers..

Sorted Set (`ZSET`): Backed by both a Hash Table (O(1) score lookup by member) and a Skip List (O(log N) range queries by score/rank). The gold standard for real-time gaming leaderboards (`ZADD`, `ZREVRANGE`), sliding-window rate limiters, and delayed job schedulers.
HyperLogLog (`PFADD`, `PFCOUNT`): Estimates unique cardinality (e.g., unique daily page visitors) with 0.81% standard error using a fixed 12 KB of memory—even for 100 million unique users!
RDB Snapshots (`BGSAVE`): Forks a child process using OS Copy-on-Write (CoW) memory pages to write a compact point-in-time binary snapshot. Fast restarts, but loses minutes of data between snapshots.
AOF (Append-Only File): Logs every write command sequentially (`appendfsync everysec`). Redis 7+ combines an RDB base snapshot with incremental AOF logs for fast recovery and minimal data loss.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Adopting appropriate design patterns around redis unlocks critical performance, scalability, and operational advantages for modern backend platforms:
bullets: **Where to Use — High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Pure caches where data can be reconstructed from the primary SQL/NoSQL database. and environments requiring Compact files, minimal disk I/O overhead during normal operation, fastest restart times..

**How to Use — Engineering Implementation**: When used for sessions, rate limits, or leaderboards, Redis needs durability across restarts and horizontal scalability beyond a single machine's RAM.. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: While essential for scalable engineering, redis introduces substantial architectural trade-offs, operational failure modes, and anti-patterns if applied inappropriately:
bullets: **Where to Avoid — Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints impose loses all writes since the last snapshot (often 5–15 minutes) on power loss; `fork()` cow can spike ram.
**Where to Avoid — Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid premature optimization when larger disk footprint and background aof rewrite i/o overhead.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Mastering redis is a defining trait of Staff-level distributed systems engineers. Navigating the delicate balance between performance, reliability, and simplicity ensures architectures scale sustainably without introducing unmanageable operational friction.
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Redis Cluster partitions the keyspace into 16,384 fixed CRC16 hash slots (`CRC16(key) % 16384`) distributed across master nodes without a central proxy.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Know the exact time complexity and internal structure of Redis `ZSET` (Hash Map + Skip List, O(log N)) and explain why `KEYS *` is forbidden in production (use `SCAN` cursor iteration instead).
